_comment: R227 identity pairs (R75 format), 2026-10-16, Claude Opus 5.5, written from the lighthouses corpus text only; no build output opened.

evidence.quote: It is owned by Trinity House.
Farne Lighthouse was one of a pair built on Inner Farne by the Corporation of Trinity House in 1811

identity_pairs.note: One organisation, England's general lighthouse authority, with and without its formal 'Corporation of' title.

evidence.quote: The lamp was also specially designed for Anvil Point by James Douglass
A further upgrade took place in 1891, supervised by the chief engineer of Trinity House, Sir James Douglass

identity_pairs.note: The same Trinity House engineer, once without and once with his title 'Sir'.

evidence.quote: with James Walker contracted to design the lighthouse
The lighthouse, a white octagonal brick tower, was designed by James Walker of civil engineers Messrs. Walker, Burgess & Cooper.

identity_pairs.note: The same lighthouse designer (civil engineer) in two articles; exact same spelling across documents.

evidence.quote: The lighthouse was designed by James Walker and built in 1835 by Olver of Falmouth, for Trinity House
Supervising the construction Henry Norris of James Walker's firm was engaged as Superintendent of the Works on behalf of Trinity House.

identity_pairs.note: The same designer of Trinity House lighthouses; second cross-document link of one person.

evidence.quote: revolving 14-panel dioptric optic by Chance Brothers & Co.
The light, a 1st Order assembly manufactured by Chance Brothers of Smethwick

identity_pairs.note: One optics manufacturer, with and without '& Co.'.

evidence.quote: Farne Lighthouse (originally named Farne High Lighthouse) is a cylindrical white tower
Whereas the High Light revolved, the Low Light showed a fixed beam from a single Argand lamp and reflector; it was monitored by the keeper at the High Lighthouse
Farne Island Lighthouse was sold on 6 June 2005 to the National Trust for £132,000

identity_pairs.note: One lighthouse under its current name, its original name, a variant ('Farne Island') and the short form 'High Light'. Trap: 'High Light' must not join the Low Light (separate pair).

evidence.quote: Trinity House also built a new lighthouse on one of the outer Farne Islands: Brownsman Island.
To the north, Trinity House maintains two operational lighthouses on the Farne Islands.

identity_pairs.note: The same island group off Northumberland named in two articles.

evidence.quote: The Old Higher Lighthouse is a disused 19th century lighthouse on the Isle of Portland, Dorset, southern England.
In 1788 Trinity House had Argand lamps installed within the higher lighthouse
In 1824 Portland High Light was improved by Trinity House

identity_pairs.note: The article's subject under its present name and its historical names 'Portland High Light' / 'Portland High'. Trap: 'Old Higher' vs 'Portland High' share almost no words.

evidence.quote: In 1911 the St Agnes lighthouse was decommissioned, having been superseded by Peninnis Lighthouse
After the closure of the lighthouse at St Agnes, Isles of Scilly in 1911

identity_pairs.note: The St Anthony's article refers to the St Agnes lighthouse by its place ('the lighthouse at St Agnes'); the closure year 1911 matches. Trap: the bare 'St Agnes' here means the lighthouse, while in the St Agnes article it can mean the island.

evidence.quote: St Mary's Lighthouse is on the tiny St Mary's (or Bait) Island, just north of Whitley Bay on the coast of North East England.
St Mary's was by then the last Trinity House lighthouse lit by oil.

identity_pairs.note: The lighthouse and its short form 'St Mary's' in one article. Trap: the island 'St Mary's Island' is a different thing (separate pair).

evidence.quote: it is sometimes known as Whitby High lighthouse (and is referred to as such on Admiralty charts)
known as the twin lights of Whitby South (the present lighthouse) and Whitby North (since demolished)
In 1890, a more efficient lamp (a powerful eight-wick mineral-oil burner) was installed in the South Light

identity_pairs.note: One surviving tower: 'Whitby Lighthouse', its chart name 'Whitby High lighthouse', and as the southern twin 'Whitby South' / 'South Light'.

evidence.quote: Trinity House offered a smaller one from their decommissioned lighthouse at Withernsea
its lantern and optic both went on to be re-used at a new lighthouse then being built at Withernsea

identity_pairs.note: Both articles mean the Withernsea lighthouse, named only by its place. Trap: a builder may keep it as a place, which is acceptable only if both mentions land on the same node.

evidence.quote: St. Anthony's lighthouse was featured in the intro of the UK version of Jim Henson's Fraggle Rock, as "Fraggle Rock Lighthouse".

identity_pairs.note: The real tower shown on television under a fictional name; one physical lighthouse. Also covers the 'St.' vs 'St' spelling.

evidence.quote: Godrevy Lighthouse (Cornish: Golowji Godrevi) was built in 1858–1859 on Godrevy Island in St Ives Bay, Cornwall.
Godrevy is still listed by Trinity House as a lighthouse, and the tower is maintained by them as a daymark.

identity_pairs.note: The lighthouse, its Cornish name, and the short form 'Godrevy'. Trap: Godrevy Island, Godrevy Head and the book 'Godrevy Light' are other things.

evidence.quote: One of those whom the lighthouse is said to have inspired was Virginia Woolf, author of To the Lighthouse
The lighthouse's visitors' book, containing the signature of Virginia Stephen (Woolf), was sold at auction

identity_pairs.note: One person under her married name and her maiden name (the text adds '(Woolf)').

evidence.quote: it was later put on display in their National Lighthouse Museum in Penzance
Following closure of the Penzance lighthouse museum, the original lens was returned to St Mary's in 2011

identity_pairs.note: The same Trinity House museum, by its name and by a description; the lens went there and came back from there.

evidence.quote: Each was equipped with a paraffin lamp and a large (first-order) fixed optic designed by Chance Brothers.
provided with large (first-order) fixed optics designed and built by James Chance

identity_pairs.note: A firm and a person who share the name Chance and do the same job (first-order fixed optics); the texts never say he is the firm. Trap: person vs firm named after a family.

evidence.quote: Originally the light was illuminated by a Douglass multi-wick mineral oil burner
supervised by the chief engineer of Trinity House, Sir James Douglass

identity_pairs.note: An apparatus named after its designer is not the designer. Trap: shared surname.

evidence.quote: was designed by James Walker of civil engineers Messrs. Walker, Burgess & Cooper.

identity_pairs.note: A person and the engineering firm that carries his name; he works for it, he is not it. Trap: person vs firm named after them.

evidence.quote: The other lighthouse on the island (Farne Low Lighthouse) was an octagonal tower, 8 m (26 ft) tall, placed 150 m (490 ft) away from the first
After the High Light had been modified and automated in 1910, use of the Low Light was discontinued

identity_pairs.note: Two towers of one pair on the same island: the High Light still stands, the Low Light was demolished. Trap: 'Farne', 'Light' and 'Lighthouse' shared.

evidence.quote: This one was built at Branscombe Hill, and the other, the Old Lower Lighthouse, on lower land.
Portland High was again made a fixed light (matching the Low Light, which had remained fixed throughout)

identity_pairs.note: The two Portland leading lights built together in 1716; different towers. Trap: 'Old ... Lighthouse' and one-letter-level name differences (Higher/Lower).

evidence.quote: St Agnes lighthouse is a 17th-century lighthouse situated on St Agnes on the Isles of Scilly.
St Agnes was chosen as it is the most westerly of the habitable islands

identity_pairs.note: The island and the lighthouse named after it. Trap: the bare name 'St Agnes' means the island here.

evidence.quote: In 1911 the St Agnes lighthouse was decommissioned, having been superseded by Peninnis Lighthouse

identity_pairs.note: Old and new light for the same waters: the successor is a different tower on another island. Trap: one replaces the other, so a builder may merge them.

evidence.quote: situated on the southern extremity of St. Mary's island
built in 1898 on St Mary's Island by the John Miller company of Tynemouth

identity_pairs.note: Two islands with the same name: St Mary's in the Isles of Scilly and St Mary's (Bait) Island off Whitley Bay, North East England. Trap: identical name, different place.

evidence.quote: known as the twin lights of Whitby South (the present lighthouse) and Whitby North (since demolished)
The North Lighthouse was then demolished

identity_pairs.note: The two Whitby twin towers: the south one survives, the north one was demolished. Trap: 'Whitby' and the pair naming.

evidence.quote: The lighthouse is a white octagonal tower, 86 feet (26 m) high
Godrevy Light by Charles Thomas and Jessica Mann describes the history of this lighthouse

identity_pairs.note: A book titled after the lighthouse, by Charles Thomas and Jessica Mann, is not the lighthouse. Trap: 'Godrevy Light' reads like a lighthouse name.

evidence.quote: In 1923 the lighthouse was purchased by the palaeobotanist, campaigner for eugenics, pioneer of birth control and Portland Museum founder Marie Stopes as a summer residence.
both the Branscombe Lodge Cottage and Stopes Cottage are now available as holiday lets

identity_pairs.note: A person and a holiday cottage named after her. Trap: shared surname.

evidence.quote: St Anthony's Lighthouse is the lighthouse at St Anthony Head, on the eastern side of the entrance to Falmouth harbour

identity_pairs.note: The headland and the lighthouse that stands on it and is named after it. Trap: place vs lighthouse named after it.
